## What this is

In this seminar we look at work on how morphological structure is planned and
computed while people are speaking. We start with the seminal work on
non-complex words and what it claims about how those words are retrieved and
produced in real time. Then we take on a series of old and new puzzles about the
productive machinery that builds complex lexical items spanning several
syntactic positions.

We also cover recent morphosyntactic theories --- Distributed Morphology and
Nanosyntax --- which already have a lot to say about how several syntactic
positions end up inside one word. In the last part of the semester we build an
experiment, run it, and analyze the results.

## What you will be able to do

1. Explain the parts of the major language production models, and the
   theoretical commitments of modern morphological theories.
2. Think critically about what formal linguistic models predict for
   psychological theories of production.
3. Find the overlooked corners of morphosyntax and morphophonology inside
   language production.
4. Come up with novel experiments that probe those corners behaviorally.
5. Connect your results or predictions to foundational questions in sentence
   production and morphology.
6. Run and analyze a behavioral experiment.

## How the course runs

**Discussion.** This is a discussion course. Readings are the primary focus, so
plan on giving each one real time.

**Bringing questions.** Before each reading day, post one question about the
reading to the ELMS thread by 11:59pm the night before. It can be about
anything in the paper. You can skip three of these with no consequence.

**Syntheses.** Three short reflections through Week 9. One question, half a page
at most, pulling together a couple of papers and our discussions. Due Sundays at
11:59pm.

**Presentations.** Everyone presents one paper from the lock-in weeks (Weeks
6--9): background, the question, the assumptions, the method and its logic, and
what the results do and do not license.

**Coding.** After fall break we get into the dirty work of experimentation.
Short weekly exercises in R and JavaScript, modifying existing code rather than
writing it from scratch. **Not graded, completely optional.**

**Project.** An experiment proposal for a production experiment in a language
other than English, including understudied dialects of English. You explain the
experiment and why it matters for the questions we ask in this course.

::: {.note}
There is no textbook. All readings are posted on **ELMS**. Read them digitally
if you can. If you would rather have something on paper, email me ahead of time
and I will print it for you.
:::
